Patient demographics:
  age: 19
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Environmental Scientist
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 36

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Arguments: Arguments, Affective Expression: Crying, Tactile (Unexpected Touch): Being touched unprepared
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation, Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building, Avoid People: avoid other people
  Threat: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel, Threat in Faces: I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat

Vignette:
Amir had always been a quiet observer, a skill he believed served him well in his work as an environmental scientist. At nineteen, he was proud of his new job and his recent marriage, milestones that felt like the start of a stable, predictable life. Yet, in the quiet moments, a different kind of observation took over, one that had nothing to do with soil samples or water tables. It was a constant, humming vigilance that left him exhausted. In meetings, he couldn't focus on the data being presented because he was too busy studying the subtle shifts in his colleagues' expressions, searching for the tightening of a jaw or the narrowing of eyes that he had come to believe was the first sign of danger. He always arrived early to secure the chair in the corner, the one with its back flush against the wall, allowing him an unobstructed view of the room and, more importantly, the door. To his colleagues, he probably just seemed reserved; to Amir, it was a matter of survival.

This way of being in the world wasn't new, but it had sharpened since he left his family home. The memories that fueled it were from a time he rarely spoke of, the years he spent living with his uncle. The house had been a landscape of emotional tripwires. An argument could erupt from nothing—a misplaced remote control, a glass set down too loudly. Amir remembers the sound of his uncle’s rising voice, a crescendo of rage that would make the air in the small living room feel thick and heavy. He learned that crying was the worst thing he could do; his own tears seemed only to pour fuel on the fire. What always came next was the sudden, searing pain of a hand grabbing his arm or the back of his neck. The touch was never gentle, never expected. It was a physical punctuation to the shouting. Before the hand ever landed, however, there was the look on his uncle’s face—a particular contortion of fury that became Amir’s only warning system. He had spent years learning to read that face, and now he couldn't stop reading it on everyone else.

These old patterns now bled into his new life with his wife, Layla. He loved her deeply, but he was terrified of her. He was terrified of the day an argument would erupt between them. To prevent this, he ceded ground on every potential disagreement, from what to have for dinner to where they should spend their holidays. This constant agreeableness, which he saw as a necessary safety measure, was beginning to look like indifference to her. He saw the confusion in her eyes when he would flinch away from her touch if he wasn't expecting it, like the time she came up behind him and put her hands on his shoulders while he was washing dishes. He had recoiled so sharply he’d almost dropped the plate. He also couldn't bear to be in their apartment alone. The silence felt menacing, a vacuum where threats could materialize. He would wait for her in the car after work rather than go inside first, a habit she found endearing at first, but which had become a source of quiet friction.

The life he was building felt increasingly fragile, managed by a complex set of rules that were invisible to everyone but him. He had stopped going out with colleagues after work, finding the unpredictability of a crowded bar unbearable. At home, he felt like a stranger, watching Layla with the same hypervigilance he applied to everyone else, trying to pre-empt a conflict that she had no intention of starting. The breaking point came last Tuesday. Layla had been crying softly while watching a film, and the sound had sent a jolt of pure panic through Amir. He’d abruptly stood up and gone into the bedroom, unable to explain the terror her sadness provoked in him. Later, she followed him, her face etched with hurt. "I don't know how to reach you," she'd whispered, her voice thick with unshed tears. "It feels like you're a million miles away." Seeing her pain, and recognizing it was a direct result of his own invisible wounds, was what finally propelled him to seek help. He was afraid of what he might have to revisit in therapy, but the fear of losing the one safe person in his life was now, finally, greater.
